title: Incredible Inventors
passages: Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519) was an Italian Renaissance GENIUS born in Vinci, a small town in Tuscany, who excelled as a PAINTER, sculptor, engineer, architect, and scientist — making him one of history's greatest polymaths. He filled over 13,000 pages of notebooks with ideas for inventions including a flying machine, a helicopter design, and an ARMORED vehicle, all sketched centuries before any were built.

His most famous painting is the Mona Lisa, still considered one of the greatest artworks ever created. Leonardo's observations of human anatomy were so detailed and accurate that they were used by medical students for over 400 years. He was a true visionary, endlessly curious about how the world worked.

Nikola Tesla (1856-1943) was a SERBIAN-American inventor who made revolutionary contributions to alternating current electricity — the system that POWERS homes and businesses worldwide today. Born in Smiljan in modern-day Croatia, Tesla immigrated to the United States in 1884 and briefly worked for Thomas Edison before a famous RIVALRY developed between the two men.

Tesla was awarded over 300 PATENTS in his lifetime, including the Tesla coil and an electric DYNAMO. Despite his genius, Tesla died nearly penniless in 1943. Today the unit of magnetic field strength is called the tesla in his honour, a fitting tribute to a brilliant but often overlooked inventor.

Marie Curie (1867-1934) was a POLISH-French scientist and the first person in history to win two Nobel Prizes — one in physics in 1903 and one in chemistry in 1911. Born Maria Sklodowska in WARSAW, she moved to Paris to study at a time when women were largely excluded from higher education.

Curie discovered two new elements: polonium, named after her homeland, and radium. Her work on radioactivity transformed our understanding of atomic structure and laid the foundation for radiation therapy, a CANCER treatment still used today. Marie Curie died in 1934 from an illness caused by decades of radiation exposure during her research in FRANCE.

Thomas Edison (1847-1931) was one of the most PROLIFIC inventors in history, holding 1,093 PATENTS — the most ever granted to a single person at the time. Born in Milan, Ohio, Edison developed a practical incandescent lightbulb in 1879, making reliable electric WIRING and lighting possible for homes and cities.

He also invented the phonograph, a device for RECORDING and playing back sound. Edison created the first industrial research laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey, pioneering TEAMWORK in invention by employing dozens of scientists. He famously said that genius is one percent inspiration and ninety-nine percent perspiration.

Orville and Wilbur Wright were American bicycle mechanics from DAYTON, Ohio who achieved the impossible on December 17, 1903: the first successful powered, controlled flight by a heavier-than-air aircraft. Their plane, the Flyer I, lifted off from the sands of Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, and Orville flew just 120 feet in 12 seconds.

The brothers spent years testing over 200 GLIDER designs and built a homemade wind TUNNEL to study aerodynamics. To get the heavy aircraft moving, they used a special LAUNCH rail. Their invention transformed travel, warfare, and trade across the entire 20th century and beyond, shrinking the world dramatically.

Ada Lovelace (1815-1852) was an ENGLISH mathematician now widely regarded as the world's first computer programmer — a remarkable achievement given that computers would not exist for another 100 years. The daughter of the famous poet Lord Byron, Ada worked with inventor Charles Babbage on his proposed Analytical ENGINE, a mechanical computing device.

In 1843 she translated a scientific paper and added her own notes, containing what is now recognised as the first algorithm ever written for a machine. Ada also had the VISION to predict that computers might one day COMPOSE music and create art. She died at just 36 years old, her genius barely recognised in her lifetime.
